Exclusions and Attendance

How much of the attendance problem is exclusion? A secondary analysis alongside How to Pull the Right Lever.

Author
Affiliation

Adam Dennett

Bartlett Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis, University College London

Published

October 22, 2026

ImportantThe question

Brighton & Hove’s council has begun asking how exclusions from secondary schools work in the city. How to Pull the Right Lever found that attendance is the single largest school-level driver of GCSE attainment, so an interest in exclusions is a reasonable thing to follow from it: excluded pupils are not in school, and a pupil not in school does not learn.

The question this note answers is narrower and more useful. Of the attendance problem that exists, how much of it is exclusion? If the answer is “most of it”, exclusions policy is attendance policy and the council should act. If the answer is “a few per cent”, then pressing schools on exclusions is a cheap substitute for the harder work, and risks moving the only lever a school fully controls in a direction that helps nobody.

1 The short answer

In 2025/26, across every state-funded secondary school in England:

  • Absence ran at 8.01% of possible sessions.
  • Sessions missed because a pupil was suspended accounted for 0.251 percentage points of that — 3.1% of all absence.
  • Illness accounted for 45.9% and unauthorised absence with no given reason for 29.4%.

If every suspension in England stopped tomorrow and none of those pupils missed a single further session, the secondary absence rate would fall from 8.01% to 7.76%. That is the entire size of the prize, and it is an upper bound rather than an estimate, because it assumes a pupil who is no longer suspended attends perfectly instead.

NoteVerdict

Exclusions are a real but small part of the attendance story, and they are a symptom of it rather than a cause of it.

They are not a red herring — the association between a school’s suspension rate and its attendance is strong and worth understanding. But the association runs overwhelmingly through the same pupils, not through the suspensions themselves: schools that suspend more have more absence of every kind, including the kinds suspension cannot touch. Treating exclusions as the attendance lever would be acting on the symptom that is easiest to count and easiest to blame a school for.

For Brighton & Hove specifically the case is weaker still. The city suspends less than most of England and has close to the worst attendance in the country. Whatever is driving absence here, it is not how often the schools suspend.

2 What the data is

Three published sources, all Open Government Licence v3.0, assembled by R/15_exclusions.R.

Three things about this are worth saying plainly before any number is quoted.

Absence here is autumn and spring terms only. That is the basis the DfE publishes early enough to reach 2025/26, and it is the basis used in the 2025/26 addendum to the main report, so the two agree. Summer-term absence is excluded for every year equally.

The exclusions collection runs a year behind. Suspensions for 2025/26 are not published until summer 2027. Everything joining exclusions to absence therefore stops at 2024/25; the absence decomposition alone runs to 2025/26.

Code E is measured from the attendance register, not inferred. The central number in this note — how many sessions suspension actually costs — is not derived by multiplying suspensions by an assumed length. It is a column in the published absence file, counted by schools as they mark the register. 3,419 secondary schools report it.

3 How big is exclusion, as a share of absence?

3.1 Every reason, ranked

Illness is the mountain. “Unauthorised, other” — the code that carries most persistent absence — is the second mountain. Suspension is the 8th largest reason a secondary pupil in England is not in a lesson, behind being late and behind unauthorised family holidays.

3.2 And it has grown

This is the honest part of the case for taking exclusions seriously. Suspension’s contribution to absence has gone from 0.145 percentage points in 2016/17 to 0.251 in 2025/26, and England’s suspension rate has risen from 9.3 per 100 pupils to 21.3. Something real is happening in school behaviour policy.

But the scale has not changed. Doubling a figure that was 2.8% of absence gets you to 3.1% of absence.

3.3 And nationally, it has risen while attendance improved

Over the four years for which both series exist, England’s secondary suspension rate rose by about half while persistent absence fell by about a fifth. That is not proof that suspensions do not matter — both series are moved by other things, and the post-COVID attendance recovery is doing most of the work on the blue line. But it is the opposite of what you would see if exclusions were the engine of the attendance problem, and anyone proposing that they are has to account for it.

4 Does a school that suspends more have worse attendance?

Yes, strongly. This is the finding that makes the council’s interest reasonable, and it deserves to be stated at full strength before it is taken apart.

The right-hand panel is the whole argument. It removes every single session that a suspension caused, and the relationship barely moves: from r = +0.60 to r = +0.52.

A school that suspends a lot is a school where a lot of pupils are absent for reasons that have nothing to do with being suspended. The suspension rate is telling you about the pupils, not doing something to them.

4.1 What survives a control for intake

Each row adds a control. The outcome throughout is absence with suspension sessions already removed, so nothing here is mechanical.

The last row is the one that matters. It carries a separate intercept for every school, so it no longer compares a school in Blackpool with a school in Surrey. It asks: when a school suspends more than it usually does, does it also have worse attendance than it usually does? That differences away everything fixed about the intake, the catchment, the building and the leadership.

The answer is yes, and it is 29% the size of the raw association. 71% of what the scatter plot shows is schools being different from each other, not suspension doing anything.

TipWhat that coefficient means in practice

A school that raises its suspension rate by 10 per 100 pupils — a large move, well beyond what most schools do in a year — is associated with 0.12 percentage points more non-suspension absence. Against a mean absence rate of around 8.0%.

And even that is an association, not an effect. The plausible mechanism runs the other way: a pupil who has disengaged both stops attending and gets suspended, and a school whose cohort is unravelling does more of both in the same year.

5 Does any of this reach attainment?

This is the step the council’s theory needs. Pulling the Right Lever established that absence is the largest school-level predictor of GCSE attainment. If exclusions matter to attainment, they should add something to that model.

Read the last two rows as the test:

  • Starting from a model that already has the suspension rate in it, adding absence raises R² by 0.113.
  • Starting from a model that already has absence in it, adding the suspension rate raises R² by 0.005.

Absence does about 25 times as much work as suspension in explaining what a school’s cohort gets at GCSE. Suspension is not worthless — the coefficient is negative and statistically significant on 12,000-odd school-years, as almost anything is at that sample size — but once you know a school’s absence rate, knowing how often it suspends tells you very nearly nothing further.

6 Brighton & Hove

6.1 The city suspends below average and attends near the bottom

This is the finding that should settle the question locally.

Brighton & Hove is the 3rd worst of 151 local authorities for secondary absence, at 10.27% against an England figure of 8.09%. On suspensions it ranks 116th — meaning 115 local authorities suspend more than it does, and it sits comfortably in the lower half of the country at 13.0 suspensions per 100 pupils against England’s 21.3.

Exclusion sessions account for 0.173 percentage points of the city’s 10.27% absence rate — about 1.7% of it, lower than the national share of 3.1%.

A city that suspends less than most of England and attends worse than almost all of it does not have an exclusions-driven attendance problem. It has an attendance problem.

6.2 Permanent exclusion is close to extinct here

Across ten secondary schools and roughly 12,800 pupils, the city permanently excluded 17 children in 2016/17, 4 in 2021/22, none at all in 2023/24, and 1 in 2024/25. Whatever problem the city has, it is not that its schools are permanently excluding children.

Note also the direction of travel. Between 2021/22 and 2024/25 the city’s suspension rate rose from 9.5 to 13.0 per 100 — and its persistent absence fell, from 31.3% to 27.2%. The two moved in opposite directions, here as nationally.

6.3 School by school

Three things stand out, and all three argue the same way.

Longhill is the one school where the mechanical effect is visible at all. It suspends far more than any other school in the city, and suspension costs it 1.00 percentage points of attendance. Against an absence rate of 16.7% and persistent absence at 47% of its pupils. Even at the city’s extreme, suspension is about 6% of the problem.

Brighton Aldridge suspends below the city average and has the city’s second-worst attendance. Its persistent absence is 42% of pupils on a suspension rate of 9.5 per 100 — a seventh of Longhill’s. The school with the best value added in the city, serving the most disadvantaged intake, is not solving its attendance problem by suspending, and is not causing it by suspending either.

Patcham reports zero suspensions, four years running. On a roll of about 1,100, in a school that recorded 193 suspensions in 2006/07. Four consecutive exact zeros is unusual enough that it may reflect recording practice as much as policy, and it would be worth the council asking — but taken at face value it is the cleanest possible test of the theory, and Patcham’s absence rate of 7.9% is good for the city without being exceptional.

7 What this does not show

Four honest limits, because the finding is only useful if it survives them.

This is about suspension, not about the children suspended. The claim here is about aggregates: suspension is a small share of total absence. For an individual child who is suspended repeatedly, the disruption is serious, the association with poor outcomes is severe, and nothing in this note argues otherwise. A policy aimed at the few hundred children in this city with repeat suspensions can be worth doing on its own merits while being irrelevant to the city’s attendance rate.

Permanent exclusion does not appear in a school’s absence at all. A permanently excluded pupil comes off the roll, so their subsequent absence belongs to alternative provision or to the next school. The figures above therefore understate exclusion’s total effect on attendance in the system — but permanent exclusion is running at 1 child a year across the whole of secondary Brighton & Hove, so the understatement is not large here.

Nor do off-rolling or managed moves. A pupil moved off a roll informally leaves no trace in either dataset. If the council’s real interest is in that, exclusions data is not where it will be found, and the school-level absence data will not find it either. This is a genuine gap and it is the one question in this area where the published data cannot answer the council.

None of the models here identify a causal effect. They establish that the association between suspension and non-suspension absence survives controls and shrinks dramatically under school fixed effects. They cannot rule out that some of what remains is causal. What they do rule out is that it is large.

8 What would be more use

If the council’s underlying concern is attendance — and on the evidence of Pulling the Right Lever it should be — then the published data points somewhere else entirely.

45.9% of secondary absence is illness and 29.4% is unauthorised with no given reason. Between them they are 75% of the problem. Persistent absence in Brighton & Hove sits at 27.2% of secondary pupils — more than one child in four missing at least a tenth of their schooling.

Three questions the same data could answer, and which nobody has asked:

  1. Which children? Persistent absence is heavily concentrated. A pupil-level view the council already holds would say whether the same children are persistently absent year on year, and what else is true of them.
  2. How far do they travel? The city’s school system work shows disadvantaged children in Brighton & Hove travel further than their classmates, and longer journeys are associated with lower attendance. That is a lever the council controls directly, through catchments and admissions, and it has never been costed against attendance.
  3. What happens to attendance after a suspension? The data to answer this is in the council’s own attendance returns, not in any DfE publication. If suspension really does start a spiral, that is where it would show up — and it would be a far better argument than the aggregate one.
ImportantThe one-line answer

Exclusions matter to the children they happen to, and they are worth understanding on their own terms. As an explanation of Brighton & Hove’s attendance problem, they are about 2% of it — in a city that already suspends less than three-quarters of England while attending worse than all but 2 local authorities in it.

If the city wants attendance to improve, exclusions are not where the work is.
